newsitem.title: USA: FEMA cushions blow from natural disasters -- S&P.
newsitem.headline: FEMA cushions blow from natural disasters -- S&P.

text.p: Natural disasters have had minimal credit impact on Standard & Poor's public finance ratings due to assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, S&P said in a report Monday.

For example, though recent severe flooding in California will generate short-term economic disruptions, no long-term adverse impact on credit quality is expected, the January 20 Standard & Poor's CreditWeek Municipal said.
To determine potential credit implications, Standard & Poor's evaluates the severity of damage, the governments affected, and the damaged property's insurance status.

The most costly recent natural disaster was the Northridge earthquake, which struck the Los Angeles, Calif., area on Jan. 17, 1994. Many rated local governments in Los Angeles County experienced substantial damage. Through the ongoing reimbursements of FEMA, no negative rating actions were taken.
The more than 80 rated entities that were affected included many redevelopment agencies, cities, school districts, and hospitals.

FEMA is responsible for coordinating a total of 27 agencies involved in the California recovery effort, which remains underway. Projected total expenditures from all federal agencies are approximately $12.5 billion. Of that amount, $7.2 billion comes directly from FEMA, with other agencies providing the balance.
Hurricane Andrew, which hit southern Florida and southern Louisiana on Aug. 24, 1992, was the nation's most expensive hurricane to date, costing FEMA and its related agencies some $2.8 billion.

By supplementing local and state relief efforts and financing a substantial portion of the rebuilding effort after a disaster, FEMA helps ease the financial strain on local governments. In addition, aid to individuals and businesses helps preserve the economic base. These factors combine to help local entities maintain credit quality.
Natural disasters' impact on state and local governments will vary depending on the size and type of governments affected.
States, for example, are better positioned to address the adverse credit impacts of major natural disasters due to larger and more diverse revenue streams.

Lease issues for local governments may be more vulnerable, especially if the project is rendered unusable and is not considered essential. In addition, tax allocation bonds with low coverage and high tax base concentration could experience adverse credit implications from a severe natural disaster, the report said.
